item.content:encoded:
Blue-stained plywood and knotted larch feature in our latest lookbook of residential interiors anchored by statement wooden staircases.

There is no end to architects' appetite for building with wood, with recent wooden projects around the world ranging from a demountable library in Amsterdam to a cedar and hempcrete chicken coop in Portugal.

The following homes also make the most of the material in their interior designs, which are defined by wooden staircases in various formations.

This is the latest in our lookbooks series, which provides visual inspiration from Dezeen's archive. For more inspiration, see previous lookbooks featuring colourful taps, scenic bathrooms and striking patios.

Cobalt Coach House, UK, by Foils

A plywood staircase forms the centrepiece of this southeast London home, tinted in a cobalt blue stain to reveal its swirly grain.

British architecture studio Foils renovated the former coach house in Peckham to create more space, which included the addition of the bespoke stair that was constructed in five parts and assembled on site.

Find out more about Cobalt Coach House ›

Wooden Annex, Mexico, by Pedro & Juana

Wooden Annex is a Mexican house extension in Valle de Bravo, which was conceived from two steel U-beams and a dried pine tree.

The interior of the staircase was also lined with pine and punched with porthole-style windows.

"You can say [that the project] served as a laboratory to prove that designing with wood in Mexico is possible, beautiful, and a more sustainable answer than the omnipresent construction with everything concrete," said architecture studio Pedro & Juana.

Find out more about Wooden Annex ›

London house, UK, by Waind Gohil and Potter Architects

Fabricated offsite and assembled like a puzzle, this boxy wooden staircase defines a small dwelling in the garden of a Shepherd's Bush home in west London.

The staircase connects all three levels of the property and was constructed entirely from an engineered-timber product with a knotted larch finish.

Find out more about this London house ›

Barn at the Ahof, the Netherlands, by Julia van Beuningen

Dutch Architectural designer Julia van Beuningen renovated this 19th-century barn in Gelderland to create a rental home with four bedrooms and a large open-plan living space.

The centrepiece of the living space is a strikingly spiralled plywood staircase, characterised by a curved geometry that offers a playful contrast to the barn's traditional wooden columns and beams.

Find out more about Barn at the Ahof ›

Light House, Croatia, by OFIS Arhitekti 

Light House is an unusual stone property on the Croatian island of Cres, which was renovated with a slatted timber framework throughout that acts as furniture and allows daylight to filter through the entire interior.

Slovenian studio OFIS Arhitekti incorporated a staircase into the striking framework, fluidly connecting the dwelling's three storeys.

Find out more about Light House ›

Casa Thomé Beira da Silva, Brazil, by Marcos Bertoldi Arquitetos

A monolithic helical staircase sits at the heart of Casa Thomé Beira da Silva, a Curitiba home by local firm Marcos Bertoldi Arquitetos.

Crafted from timber, the stepped structure is flanked by latticed wooden screens that filter daylight into the open-plan interior.

Find out more about Casa Thomé Beira da Silva ›

The Arbor House, Scotland, by Brown & Brown

Scottish architecture studio Brown & Brown married stone salvaged from a dilapidated farmstead with wood and board-marked concrete to bring The Arbor House to life.

Located in a conservation area in Aberdeen, the house has a dining and circulation space with a tightly twisted birch plywood staircase.

"The stair was assembled over three weeks as timber treads were individually cut and hand-layered to form a smooth, sinuous parabolic curve," said Brown & Brown.

Find out more about The Arbor House ›

London house, UK, by Paolo Cossu Architects

An extra-wide staircase designed to give residents a place to sit, chat or read features in this east London home by local studio Paolo Cossu Architects.

Crafted from chunky wooden blocks, the stair is connected to matching oak bookshelves that cover the adjacent wall.

Find out more about this London house ›

item.content:encoded:
Architect Kristijan Markoc has created a downloadable template for a "deliberately modest", two-bedroom timber home designed to be adapted to any site.

Named Plana House, the replicable home design has a compact, 42-square-metre plan and is composed of a simple, pitched-roof structure that can be constructed using readily-available materials.

The home was designed by Markoc, who is founder of Swiss studio Plana Architecture, to be a more-accessible alternative to typical housing designs, prioritising affordability, adaptability and a straight-forward construction process.

Central to this idea was bringing residents back into the process of building a home, leading to Markoc's creation of freely-available technical drawing sets for the project.

Resource for people to "adapt and potentially build their own house"

"Traditionally, much of the knowledge needed to build a house was held in common by the people and communities who built and inhabited them," Markoc told Dezeen.

"Plana House seeks to place some of that knowledge back in the commons by making a complete set of architectural drawings freely available, so that people can use it as a resource to understand, adapt and potentially build their own house."

Markoc, who has plans to build a prototype of Plana House, drew on his knowledge of modular construction for the structure, which he designed in line with UK and Irish construction regulations.

Although the structure is adaptable, any construction of Plana House would still need to be reviewed by a licensed architect or qualified professional to meet local building regulations, Markoc explained.

"The house uses a simple timber frame based on a highly efficient structural grid, developed using my experience with modular construction methods to make the building as efficient and economical as possible," Markoc explained.

"All dimensions, details, and construction methods must be verified and adapted by a licensed architect or qualified professional to ensure compliance with local building regulations, site conditions, and applicable standards prior to construction," he added.

Renders of the design by Markoc showcase a simple, single-storey timber frame clad entirely with timber panels, which can be built from standard, off-the-shelf materials.

Externally, the structure is intended to be finished in a variety of materials depending on what is locally available. For flexibility, the home can be built atop screw piles or pad foundations for a light-touch approach.

Read:

Woonpioniers models adjoining Dutch homes on "a game of Tetris"

"[The structure] relies on readily available materials that can be purchased in any local hardware store, while its simple and familiar form allows it to sit naturally within very different regional contexts, with cladding materials adapted according to the local climate, availability and budget," Markoc said.

Inside, the home's rectangular plan is split into two wings, containing an open-plan living, dining and kitchen area at one end, and two bedrooms and a bathroom at the other.

A series of windows draw light into the interior, where the pitched roof helps to create more-spacious feel within the four-metre-wide spaces.

Elsewhere, Woonpioniers completed a pair of interlocking houses for two families within a single gabled volume in Utrecht.

The renders are by Tom Stepins.

Dezeen School Shows: black leather modular boots informed by punk culture are among the projects from Häme University of Applied Sciences.

Also featured are woven shoes with 3D-printed soles and shoes made from tanned vegetable leather.

Häme University of Applied Sciences

Course: Smart and Sustainable Design Bachelor's degree

School statement:

"Häme University of Applied Sciences (HAMK) is shaping the next generation of material‑driven designers in our Smart and Sustainable Design Bachelor's degree programme, where forward‑looking experimentation, craft heritage and contemporary design thinking meet.

"Rooted in Finland's long tradition of material innovation, our programme encourages students to push the boundaries of form, technique and sustainable making.

"This selection presents emerging designers and their work from our footwear programme, showcasing a wide range of approaches within the discipline – from traditional handcraft and material investigation to functional footwear and forward-thinking modular design.

"Häme University of Applied Sciences (HAMK) is the only university in the Nordic countries where you can study footwear design.

"Each project expresses a unique design voice and demonstrates a strong interest in exploring new directions in footwear through sustainability, technology and upcycling.

"Supported by dedicated footwear design studios, a variety of materials, tools and technologies for experimentation, our emerging designers are guided by experienced staff as they develop, prototype and produce their own footwear.

"Through practical making and innovative design processes, they are empowered to become creative changemakers and help shape a more sustainable future for footwear."

Cult of Craft: Louise by Heidi Kannisto

"Louise shoes bring together the dimensions of traditional weaving and contemporary 3D modelling. The design process combines a creative, ragged upper with a meticulously refined sole built through 3D modelling.

"The shoe's exterior is playful and draws inspiration from late-90s pop culture as well as the design language of traditional, colourful rag rugs designed from upcycled materials.

"The shoe is designed to be glue-free and versatile. The upper can be attached to the sole in various ways, and at the end of its lifespan, it can be taken apart and the parts recycled properly."

Student: Heidi Kannisto
Course: Footwear Design and Development Bootcamp
Email: kannistoheidi[at]email.com

Mod by Lauri Leino, Sittichok Moungmee, Riko Kuokkanen, Miia Lilli and Georg Lichtenberg

"Traditional footwear design often leads to excessive waste, as worn-out or damaged shoes are frequently discarded rather than repaired.

"To rethink traditional footwear waste, we developed a modular shoe to combat the waste generated by the footwear industry, where millions of shoes end up in landfills each year due to reparable wear or fast fashion trends.

"By designing shoes with interchangeable and replaceable parts, we sought to create a more sustainable alternative that allows consumers to repair or customise their footwear instead of discarding it entirely."

Students: Lauri Leino, Sittichok Moungmee, Riko Kuokkanen, Miia Lilli and Georg Lichtenberg
Course: Emil Aaltonen Museum Collaboration Project

BarbieBoon by Selma Repo

"This project was made in the Erasmus BIP course at the Estonian Academy of Arts. There we disassembled sneakers from factories, which were going to the landfill and designed them to fit upon clog soles.

"In these shoes, I wanted to mix up two worlds – where the sporty world meets classy high heels – like childhood Barbie would have done.

"The style is a play with sneakers' already existing shapes and keeping the style flowy and constructive."

Student: Selma Repo
Course: From Sneaker to Clog, Erasmus BIP
Email: selma.s.repo[at]gmail.com

Modular Shoe by Yan Wu

"This footwear project originated from my experience of discarding a pair of shoes because the sole was damaged, even though the upper remained in good condition.

"Reflecting on how modern shoes permanently glue together the sole, upper and lining, I recognised the difficulty of repair and replacement, which shortens product lifespan and increases waste.

"Inspired by the structural logic of traditional Chinese straw sandals, I reinterpreted their weaving and lacing system through contemporary materials and manufacturing methods.

"The design separates the sole, upper and lining into independent modules that can be removed and replaced individually, creating a more adaptable and sustainable footwear framework."

Student: Yan Wu
Course: Footwear Design and Development Bootcamp
Email: apus7702[at]gmail.com

Footwear Collection by Dorota Kaňuchová

"I see myself as a designer who likes to take on challenges and is passionate about exploring the intersection of concept, craft and technology.

"For me, footwear is a form of self-expression and storytelling, which is why my work tends to be diverse. I approach each project individually, so I always follow what it needs."

Student: Dorota Kaňuchová
Course: Personnel Design Project
Email: dorotakanuchova[at]gmail.com

Ketara by Riko Kuokkanen

"This is the result of my thesis in the Smart and Sustainable Design programme – handmade barefoot shoes made of thick vegetable-tanned leather.

"The product was 3D-modelled and printed by myself. I aimed to combine traditional handcrafted shoemaking with durable materials."

Student: Riko Kuokkanen
Course: Thesis
Email: riko.kuokkanen[at]outlook.com

Kroko by Miia Lilli

"This was the first Miia Lilli shoe I ever made. I chose to challenge myself by creating a high heel instead.

"I was inspired by unusual textures and experimented with manipulating the leather to create a rich, tactile surface. I also developed the elongated last shape to give the Kroko shoe a bold and elegant silhouette."

Student: Miia Lilli
Course: Materials and Techniques in Fashion
Email: miialilli[at]icloud.com

The Clowd Slippers by Senja Kaukonen

"The Clowd slippers are inspired by a flower-like form of a ceramic artwork by Anne-Sophie Boulogne. The design is zero-waste because they are made of second-hand denim, and they are filled with fabric waste.

"Their name comes from their imaginative three-dimensional shape and cartoonishly big size. The biggest challenge in the design process was figuring out the way to make the rounded shapes on the upper."

Student: Senja Kaukonen
Course: Basics of Fashion 1
Email: senja.kaukonen[at]dnainternet.net

Unisex Mini Collection for a Streetwear Brand SS25 by Mailis Purho

"My design is a classic combat boot style combined with eye-catching removable accessories that wrap around the shoe.

"The combination of deep black leather, chrome hardware and a pop of red creates a bold and timeless look.

"The O-ring straps add edge and personality to the piece, and I made them removable for a modular approach. Lowered ankle makes the design more casual and suitable for everyday use.

"The design is inspired by alternative fashion based on the New York downtown scene, which is influenced by subcultures like punk rock and metal. The design language communicates rebellion, freedom, and self-expression."

Student: Mailis Purho
Course: Prototyping and Techniques in Fashion
Email: mailis.purho[at]gmail.com

item.content:encoded:
Canada's Ivy Studio has transformed a 1970s bank into a veterinary clinic for exotic animals in Laval, Quebec, featuring minimalist interiors and soft lighting.

The Fauna clinic occupies a standalone structure completed in a brutalist style near the waterfront, just over the Prairies River northwest of Montreal.

Ivy Studio leaned into the building's existing style to inform the interiors, creating a calm, minimalist environment for the patients and their handlers.

"By celebrating its historical shell, Fauna establishes a unique dialogue between imposing institutional architecture and the compassionate, soothing nature of veterinary care," the studio said.

The building spans 380 square metres over two levels, with the public areas and treatment facilities housed across the ground floor.

Boasting 16-foot (4.9-metre) ceilings, the reception and waiting areas maximise natural light from the building's existing windows.

The original concrete coffered ceiling is left exposed and painted a deep brown, contrasting concrete flooring and the warm grey of the textured plaster walls.

Facing the waiting area, the four consultation rooms are arranged in an offset row through the centre of the plan.

Each is faced with a curved wall that sweeps up to the tall ceiling, mimicking the building's exterior, and is also denoted by vertical partitions with stepped end-profile details.

"This dramatic gesture provides intimacy for the consultation rooms while serving as a sculptural focal point from the waiting area," said Ivy Studio.

Fluted glass doors slide open to access the consultation rooms, which feature walnut desks with chrome bases, matching the waiting room benches and the reception counter.

The individual rooms all link to the treatment area behind, where a spiral staircase leads down to office, storage and research space in the basement.

Read:

Ivy Studio converts historic bank building into offices for Montreal ad agency

Careful consideration was given to the lighting design, comprising diffused light boxes inside the consultation rooms along with the natural illumination in the other public spaces.

"A soothing environment is paramount for an exotic animal clinic, where patients are easily stressed," Ivy Studio said. "The lighting strategy in the public zones is soft, dimmed, and strictly indirect."

In the treatment room and basement, the building's concrete bones are exposed, and the fluted concrete walls are painted soft cream.

The bank's original vault is repurposed as a closed pharmacy and lab – the finishing touch in adapting the former financial institution into a contemporary medical facility.

Ivy Studio is perhaps best known for its hospitality projects across Canada, with completed restaurant projects ranging in style from Japanese minimalism to colourfully retro and bold and glamorous.

The studio's commercial portfolio includes a dry cleaners modelled on a Parisian apartment, an all-black spinning studio and offices for a digital advertising agency also housed in a former bank.

The photography is by Alex Lesage.

Project team: Gabrielle Rousseau, David Kirouac, Guillaume B Riel, Philip Staszewski, Vincent Maillé, Sandra Zimmerman
Construction: Groupe Manovra

item.content:encoded:
A cluster of monolithic forms lined with grey brick and built into a steep bank defines Tollymore, a riverside house in Northern Ireland by Belfast studio McGonigle McGrath.

Located off a narrow road in County Down, Tollymore comprises six rectangular forms set at different levels across its steep site, which the studio said helps to "make it part of the landscape".

According to McGonigle McGrath, this design is a direct result of a "well-developed brief" set out by the client, in which they imagined a home divided into small "pods" that maximise views of nature and sounds of the adjacent river.

"It was a unique brief and a fantastic site, and between that and the client's enthusiasm at a particularly creative time in the practice, this design emerged as a new way of making spaces," studio principal Kieran McGonigle told Dezeen.

Each of Tollymore's volumes is raised on a stepped plinth formed from board-marked concrete. As they cascade down the sloped site, the roofline is at the same level, meaning the volumes differ in scale.

Between them are walkways, covered passages and courtyards, giving rise to an arrangement intended to evoke water flowing around the stones in the river.

The six blocks include two living areas, three sleeping zones and one that can be used as either.

Moving between the bedrooms and living spaces brings the family briefly outside, which is "a ritual experience of the views and sounds of the river, mountains and sky, whatever the weather", said the studio.

While each volume has a unique function, they were all designed to be flexible to adapt to the family's changing needs and ensure usability well into the future.

"When the children are at college, and the block that is currently an Airbnb let is not being used, the clients can close down three of the six blocks, significantly increasing the running costs of the building," said McGonigle.

Read:

Arquitecturia designs Catalan house as cluster of pavilions around garden

Tollymore's monolithic structures are clad in grey brick walls and granite-gravel roofs, which, combined with the board-marked concrete plinths, are intended to evoke boulders.

"The material choices reinforce a sense of belonging by grounding the site within its place," explained McGonigle.

Inside, the interiors contrast the rock-like exterior with warm hardwoods and exposed wooden beams, alongside terrazzo and lime-washed plaster details.

Windows are also framed in hardwood, helping to establish a "transition to the warm interior". These also maximise outward views, either to the outdoors or other rooms.

McGonigle McGrath was founded by McGonigle with Aidan McGrath in 2012. In 2019, its project House Lessans in rural Northern Ireland won RIBA House of the Year.

Another house by the studio is Hill House, a similarly monolithic home that draws on the shapes and colours of local masonry buildings in Belfast.

The photography is by Johan Dehlin.
